title: Is this progress control appropriate?
blurb: Judge whether progress monitoring, reporting and exception handling in a scenario are fit for purpose, and pick the reason that explains the verdict.
question: Larkspur Rail's finance director wants a ten-page monthly written report. The project manager offers a project dashboard reviewed at each progress review instead. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?

teach.body: Test progress control four ways. Focus: does it watch what is delivered, through burn charts, rather than spend against a zero-tolerance budget? Visibility: are dashboards pulled, updated in the right workshops, and co-created by the teams? Fit: is the chart right for the level, burn-down for a team's iteration, burn-up for the project, a CFD for bottlenecks? Exceptions: is a forecast breach of tolerance taken to the board quickly, while variation within tolerance is handled by flexing scope?

teach.body: Velocity forecasts future progress empirically, but only on the assumption that conditions stay the same. A team whose velocity swings widely gives a less certain forecast, and the forecast must use that team's own figures. A rising scope line on a burn-up pushes the finish later. Variation inside tolerance is handled by the team flexing Should and Could items; only a forecast breach of tolerance becomes an exception for the board.

teach.h: When scope grows on a burn-up
teach.caption: At 26 points per iteration the original scope would be met at about iteration 8.5; the step to 260 points pushes the forecast to iteration 10.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Larkspur Rail's Fair Fares app
teach.body: Finance director Dominic Faraday asks for a Gantt chart and a ten-page monthly report. Project manager Rhys Pengelly instead sets up a project dashboard with release status, a burn-up, current risks and issues and Agilometer trends, reviewed at each progress review, and agile coach Priyanka Desai works with Dominic on why. Each team designs its own team dashboard, and Rhys asks the app team before joining its stand-ups. Because the app team's velocity swings from 18 to 34, Rhys shows the forecast as a range.

steps.label: Reason
steps.sub: Choose the one that explains this case

teach.text: Traps: 'the team dashboard replaces checkpoint reports' is true but does not explain a change to board reporting, which is the project dashboard's job. 'CFDs reveal bottlenecks' is true but does not make a CFD the board's main project view. 'The PM pulls information from teams' is true but does not let the PM join stand-ups without the team's agreement. Within tolerance, flex scope; do not raise an exception.

items: Fit for purpose = watching delivery, pulled dashboards, right chart for the level, timely exceptions.
Project dashboard for the board, updated in progress reviews; team dashboards co-created by teams.
PM attends stand-ups with the team's agreement; dashboards are pulled, not pushed.
Velocity forecasts if conditions stay the same; scope growth moves the finish.
Inside tolerance: flex Should and Could. Forecast breach: options, then exception report.

summary: You can now judge whether progress monitoring and reporting in a scenario are fit for purpose, from dashboards and stand-ups to burn charts, velocity forecasts and exceptions. You can also pick the reason that explains the verdict rather than a true statement beside the point.

A.q: Larkspur Rail's project manager designs one team dashboard layout and tells all three delivery teams to use it unchanged, so that every dashboard looks the same. How well does this apply the progress practice, and why?
options: Well, because consistent dashboards help the board
Well, because the PM pulls information from them
Poorly, because team dashboards replace highlight reports
Poorly, because each team should co-create its own dashboard
A.why: Team dashboards support transparency and self-management and are co-created by each team, not dictated (Table 13.8).

whyNot.0: The board uses the project dashboard; imposing one team layout undermines the teams' ownership of theirs.
whyNot.1: The PM does pull from team dashboards, but that does not justify dictating their design.
whyNot.2: Team dashboards replace checkpoint reports; the project dashboard replaces highlight reports.

A.q: Easterholm County Council's assistant director, who sits on the project board, refuses to look at dashboards and insists on written monthly highlight reports. The project manager believes this is holding back agile ways of working across the department. Which role is BEST placed to tackle this?
options: The team coach
The agile coach
Project support
The product owner
A.why: The agile coach works across the organization to remove systemic blockers to agile adoption, such as a board member resisting dashboards (Table 7.2).

whyNot.0: The team coach works with one or two teams on self-management, not with board members.
whyNot.2: Project support helps with administration and dashboards but does not coach senior leaders.
whyNot.3: The product owner manages a team's product backlog, not board members' reporting habits.

A.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's head of internal audit asks how the board will know, between stage boundaries, whether the click and collect project is still on track. Which answer BEST reflects PRINCE2 Agile?
options: Through the end project report produced at closure
Through weekly checkpoint reports from each team
Through the lessons report written after each release
Through the project dashboard and progress reviews
A.why: The project dashboard replaces the highlight report; it is updated and reviewed in progress review workshops and the board pulls information from it at any time (Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: The end project report comes at closure, far too late for control between stage boundaries.
whyNot.1: Checkpoint reports, replaced by team dashboards, go from teams to the PM, not to the board.
whyNot.2: The lessons report shares lessons; it does not show whether the project is on track.

B.q: On Draycott's project burn-up, the scope line stepped up at iteration 5 after stakeholders added dashboard features, while the completed-work line has kept rising at the same rate. What is the MOST LIKELY effect?
options: The forecast completion moves later
The team's velocity has dropped sharply
The team is now ahead of its plan
Total risk exposure has now fallen
B.why: A burn-up shows completed work against total scope; when scope rises and the rate of completion is unchanged, the forecast finish moves later (12.4.3).

whyNot.1: The completed line rises at the same rate, so velocity has not changed.
whyNot.2: More scope with the same rate of delivery puts the team further from finishing, not ahead.
whyNot.3: A burn-up does not show risk exposure; that is the cumulative risk burn-down.

B.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's service design team is a little behind on its burn-down mid-iteration, but the release is still forecast to be delivered within tolerance by flexing two Could have items. The project manager wants to send an exception report to the board straight away. What should happen instead?
options: Send the exception report now
Extend the iteration by a week
Ask the board to rebaseline the release map
Let the team flex scope within tolerance
B.why: An exception occurs only when tolerances are forecast to be exceeded; within tolerance the team focuses on the highest priorities and flexes Should and Could items (Table 12.1, 12.4.3).

whyNot.0: No tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, so there is no exception to report.
whyNot.1: Timeboxes are fixed; time has zero tolerance, so what is delivered flexes instead.
whyNot.2: Rebaselining is a board response to an exception, and there is none here.

B.q: Callowmere University's pro vice-chancellor sits on the project board and asks the project manager for a detailed weekly written report, although the web team already keeps an online team dashboard. What is the BEST response?
options: Ask the web team to email her its checkpoint reports
Offer her the project dashboard and progress reviews
Send her a copy of the daily log each week
Replace the release map with a weekly Gantt chart
B.why: The project dashboard replaces the highlight report for the board; it is updated in progress review workshops and board members can pull from it whenever they need (Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: Checkpoint reports, now team dashboards, are for the PM, not the board.
whyNot.2: The daily log is the PM's informal diary, not a progress report for the board.
whyNot.3: The release map is the agile plan; a Gantt chart would replace it with detailed up-front scheduling.

C.q: Larkspur Rail's finance director wants a monthly written report of at least ten pages. Project manager Rhys Pengelly proposes instead a project dashboard showing release status, burn charts, current risks and issues and Agilometer trends, updated at each progress review and open to the board at any time. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the project dashboard replaces the highlight report
Yes, because team dashboards replace the checkpoint reports
No, because board members need written reports for control
No, because dashboards should be sent to the board monthly
C.why: The project dashboard replaces the highlight report; it is updated in progress review workshops and the board pulls information from it (Table 12.1, 12.3.2.1).

whyNot.1: This is true, but it concerns team-to-PM reporting, not what the board receives.
whyNot.2: The board keeps control through the project dashboard, progress reviews and exception reports.
whyNot.3: Dashboards are pulled by the board when needed, not pushed on a fixed cycle.

C.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's project manager decides that the e-commerce team's cumulative flow diagram will be the board's main view of progress across the whole click and collect project. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
options: Yes, because a CFD reveals bottlenecks in the workflow
Yes, because the board pulls information from the PM
No, because a CFD is used mostly at team level
No, because a CFD is a tool for Scrum teams
C.why: A cumulative flow diagram shows tasks in each workflow state and is used mostly at team level; project progress against the deadline is better shown by a burn-up on the project dashboard (12.4.2, 12.4.3).

whyNot.0: CFDs do reveal bottlenecks, but that does not make one team's CFD the right project-level view.
whyNot.1: The board pulls from the project dashboard; that does not explain why a team CFD fits the project level.
whyNot.3: CFDs are associated with flow-based working such as Kanban; the problem is the level, not the framework.

C.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's project manager forecasts when Release 3 will be complete from the service design team's average velocity over its last six iterations. She shows the forecast as a burn-up on the project dashboard, noting that it assumes conditions stay the same. Is this an appropriate application of the progress practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the digital team's velocity is higher
Yes, because velocity forecasts if conditions hold
No, because forecasts should come from the PM's view
No, because velocity belongs in the lessons report
C.why: Velocity, the average rate of story points per timebox, can forecast future progress empirically, assuming conditions remain the same; a burn-up suits the project level (Glossary, 12.4.3).

whyNot.0: Another team's velocity is irrelevant to this team's forecast.
whyNot.2: An empirical forecast from measured velocity is preferred to a personal prediction.
whyNot.3: Velocity is a progress metric for forecasting, not something reserved for the lessons report.

reteach.title: Running a charity fun run
reteach.question: A charity is organizing a fun run with a fixed date and budget. Which ways of keeping the trustees informed are sensible, and which would you challenge?

blocks.body: Sensible: a shared online board the trustees can look at any time, showing sign-ups against target, sponsors secured and open problems, reviewed at a short monthly meeting. Each volunteer team keeps its own task board, in a layout it chose. If sign-ups are forecast to miss the minimum, the organizer looks at options at once and tells the trustees. Challenge: a 20-page report every month, or volunteers being told how to lay out their boards.

blocks.text: Spending on budget tells the trustees little when the budget cannot move. What they need to see is whether enough runners and sponsors are coming in.

explain.body: Time and cost have zero tolerance, so tracking them against tolerance adds little. The aspect that flexes is what is delivered, which burn charts show at every level.

test.q: Easterholm County Council's project manager proposes that weekly spend against the fixed grant budget should be the main measure of progress reported to the board. What is the BEST criticism?
options: Spend should be reported in the lessons log
What is delivered is the measure that matters
The grant body should set the progress measure
Spend is tracked in the team dashboards instead
test.why: With zero tolerance on cost and time, flexibility in what is delivered is the primary aspect of interest, so burn charts are the main progress measure (12.3.1).

whyNot.0: The lessons log records lessons, not progress measures.
whyNot.2: The grant body's reporting needs do not change what PRINCE2 Agile treats as the key progress measure.
whyNot.3: Moving spend tracking to team dashboards still misses the point that delivery is what flexes.

explain.body: Dashboards are pulled, not pushed. Team dashboards are co-created by each team. The PM may attend daily stand-ups with the team's agreement.

test.q: Draycott's project manager asks the software team whether she may sit in on its daily stand-ups for one sprint; the team agrees. How well does this apply the progress practice?
options: Well, as she attends with the team's agreement
Well, as the PM chairs every team meeting
Poorly, as the PM uses checkpoint reports
Poorly, as the PO decides who joins stand-ups
test.why: The project manager may attend daily stand-ups with the delivery team's agreement (Table 12.1).

whyNot.1: The PM does not chair team meetings; teams self-manage their own events.
whyNot.2: Checkpoint reports are replaced by team dashboards; attending with agreement is still allowed.
whyNot.3: Attendance needs the delivery team's agreement, which the PM asked for and got.

explain.body: Burn-down for a team's work left in an iteration; burn-up for completed work at project level; a CFD, mostly at team level, for bottlenecks; a cumulative risk burn-down for risk exposure.

test.q: Callowmere University's board wants a chart showing how much of the Student Support Hub has been completed against the Welcome Week deadline, release by release. The project manager offers the web team's daily burn-down. How well does this fit, and why?
options: Well, because a burn-down shows outstanding work
Well, because the board pulls from team charts
Poorly, because a burn-up suits the project level
Poorly, because burn charts are for Kanban teams
test.why: A burn-up shows completed work against a deadline at project or product level; a burn-down usually shows a team's work left within an iteration (12.4.3).

whyNot.0: A burn-down does show outstanding work, but at team level within an iteration, not across releases.
whyNot.1: The board pulls from the project dashboard, which should carry a project-level chart.
whyNot.3: Burn charts are used at every level in PRINCE2 Agile, whatever the framework.

explain.h: Test 4: exceptions at the right moment
explain.body: Within tolerance, teams flex Should and Could items. When a tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, hold an immediate meeting on options and send an exception report to the board.

test.q: Pinewick's release burn-up now forecasts that click and collect cannot be live in all 85 stores before Easter, which is beyond tolerance. The project manager decides to report it at the next stage boundary in four weeks. What is the BEST criticism?
options: The team should extend the release past Easter
Store lockers should be added to make up time
The forecast breach needs an exception report now
The highlight report should be skipped this month
test.why: When tolerances are forecast to be exceeded, an immediate meeting considers options and the board is informed through an exception report, not at the next boundary (Table 12.1).

whyNot.0: Time has zero tolerance; the team cannot simply move the deadline.
whyNot.1: Adding scope would make the breach worse; lockers are the part the board allowed to flex.
whyNot.3: Skipping regular reporting does not address the forecast breach of tolerance.
